conventions.convention: The ambient geometry is a smooth, boundaryless, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature (−,+,+,+), with its torsion-free metric-compatible connection. Indices run from 0 through 3.
R(X,Y)Z = ∇X∇YZ − ∇Y∇XZ − ∇[X,Y]Z; R(∂c,∂d)∂b = Rᵃ_bcd ∂a. Lowering preserves slot order, Ric_bd = gᵃᶜR_abcd, S = gᵇᵈRic_bd, and G_ab = Ric_ab − Sg_ab/2.

A Jacobi field is a smooth pullback tangent-bundle section satisfying D_s²J = R(T,J)T along an affinely parametrized geodesic; the parameter need not be proper time. Included endpoints use one-sided derivatives.
The normal index form uses a future unit timelike geodesic, g(T,T)=−1, continuous piecewise-C¹ normal fields with both endpoint values zero, and no conjugate instant anywhere in (a,b], including b.

Local maximality means maximality among fixed-endpoint, piecewise-C¹ future timelike curves sufficiently C¹-close in the specified finite chart-and-partition data. Equality permits strictly increasing reparametrizations. No global or post-conjugate maximality is asserted.

Free-fall families use proper-time tangents U with g(U,U)=−c². Tidal acceleration is the infinitesimal field D_s²J, not finite-pair coordinate acceleration. Conclusions are conditional on the adopted smooth test-body model and use no empirical premises.

In length coordinates x⁰=ct, metric components are dimensionless, Christoffel coefficients have inverse-length units, and curvature, Ricci, scalar and Einstein components have inverse-length-squared units. General-chart component dimensions depend on the coordinate Jacobians.

load_bearing.statement: For the metric-selected connection on a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, R is a smooth (1,3)-tensor, Rᵃ_bcd = ∂cΓᵃ_db − ∂dΓᵃ_cb + Σe(Γᵃ_ceΓᵉ_db − Γᵃ_deΓᵉ_cb), and in a point-normal chart R_abcd(p) = (g_ad,bc + g_bc,ad − g_bd,ac − g_ac,bd)(p)/2.
The lowered curvature satisfies R_abcd = −R_bacd = −R_abdc, R_abcd = R_cdab, and R_abcd + R_acdb + R_adbc = 0. Ricci and Einstein tensors are symmetric.

For a smooth two-parameter map, (D_tD_r−D_rD_t)V = R(T,J^F)V. For affinely parametrized geodesic fibres, D_tJ^F = D_rT and D_t²J^F = R(T,J^F)T. Along any smooth geodesic, arbitrary initial value and initial covariant derivative determine a unique smooth Jacobi field on its interval; the space has dimension eight. For Jacobi fields, g(J,γ′) is affine.
Rᵃ_bcd;e + Rᵃ_bde;c + Rᵃ_bec;d = 0; ∇ᵃRic_ab = ∇bS/2, and consequently ∇ᵃG_ab = 0 for every b. This does not assert ∇cG_ab = 0.

For s₁>0 with s₁v in the exponential domain, the Jacobi field J_u along γ(t)=exp_p(tv) with initial data (0,u) satisfies d(exp_p)_{tv}(tu)=J_u(t) for 0≤t≤s₁. The kernel at s₁v is s₁{u:J_u(s₁)=0}, and its dimension equals conjugate multiplicity.

For a smooth future unit timelike geodesic γ:[a,b]→M with no conjugate instant in (a,b], A''=CA, A(a)=0, A'(a)=I has invertible A(s) for a<s≤b. Θ=A'A⁻¹ is symmetric, Θ'=C−Θ², and I(J)=∫|J'−ΘJ|² for continuous piecewise-C¹ normal fields vanishing at both endpoints. I(J)=0 if and only if J=0.
An algebraic curvature tensor at a point of a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold vanishes if R(T,J)T=0 for every timelike T and every tangent vector J.

concerns.concern: Definition (c) allows any open interval J₀ with nonempty interior, but then uses F(0,s); 0∈J₀ is not required. It also defines the variation field as ∂rF(r,s) along F(0,s), without evaluating r at 0. As written, the base curve can be undefined, and the derivative can belong to a different tangent fibre.

Definition (d), after allowing arbitrary s₀<s₁ and setting p=γ(s₀), v=γ′(s₀), says conjugacy is measured by the exponential derivative 'at s₁v'. The required vector is (s₁−s₀)v. On a unit-speed equator in the sphere product, choose s₀=1 and s₁=1+π: the instants are conjugate, but the differential at (1+π)v is nonsingular. The cited exponential-map lemma uses a base instant of 0.

The clause references to thm-gr-jacobi-equation-and-geodesic-deviation are displaced: (c) cites theorem clause (c) for variation fields being Jacobi, which is clause (b); (d) cites clause (d) for initial-value uniqueness and dimension, which is clause (c).

Fact L3 says 'for a field J along γ, g(J,T) is affine'. The cited theorem requires J to be Jacobi. For the permitted smooth field J(s)=s²T(s), g(J,T)=−s². The missing Jacobi hypothesis makes this fact false as written, although the proof uses the corresponding assertion only for Jacobi fields.

Proof step 5.1 ends its opening sentence with tags, then continues through separate paragraphs and display blocks before repeating its tags. This violates the required single-paragraph complete-step layout. The same step says 'letting ε↓a' for an integration cutoff a+ε; the limit must be ε↓0. The endpoint extension argument itself supplies the needed finite limit.

Fact L2 says 'R is a tensor, so a component identity proved in one chart holds in every chart'. Tensoriality preserves tensor identities, not arbitrary coordinate-component formulas. For example, rescaling θ to y¹=2θ changes the lowered R₁₂₁₂ component by a factor 1/4. The actual computations are correctly restricted to the displayed product chart, but the cited general inference is overstrong.

Clause (c) passes from the proved algebraic implication for all U and J to 'the tidal response of all free-fall congruences detects exactly the curvature'. The proof does not explicitly establish local realization of arbitrary separation values J and normalized future timelike directions U by the defined proper-time geodesic families. A short construction using smoothly varied initial points and normalized initial velocities would close this inference.

The maximum-scope paragraph says the results concern 'a fixed exponential chart'. The actual local-maximum theorem deliberately uses a finite family of compatible local exponential inverse branches and allows repeated spacetime events. Its hypotheses do not supply one injective exponential chart containing the whole segment.

alerts.finding: Fact L3 says 'R is a smooth tensor field, so a component identity proved in one chart holds in every chart', citing thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula. The supplier establishes tensorial transformation, not preservation of arbitrary component formulas. Coordinate rescaling changes nonzero lowered curvature components. The item's chart-specific computations and invariant zero-tensor conclusions must be distinguished from this unrestricted assertion.

Definition (a) states the curvature decomposition 'with C the Weyl tensor ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]])'. That supplier defines Riemann, Ricci, scalar and Einstein tensors, but neither defines Weyl curvature nor proves this decomposition. The consumer subsequently uses 'Weyl-type' and 'Weyl symmetries' without stating the zero-trace condition there. The reconstruction formula and its later justification do not make the earlier citation faithful; the geometric Weyl tensor can be defined locally by the displayed subtraction with its trace condition made explicit.

Tensor-slot conventions, positive rest-space metric, observer projection and unit-observer pairing are used consistently. The arbitrary-length reverse-Cauchy–Schwarz inequality follows by normalizing the timelike vector in the cited unit-vector statement.
Explicit metrics have the stated signature and time orientation. Cylindrical radius excludes zero; sphere polar formulas are confined to their regular chart.
Christoffel and geodesic computations use the metric-selected connection and affine parameter. The sphere conjugacy example is explicitly spacelike and does not invoke the timelike maximum.
Constant identity-chart arrays define smooth tensor fields; the counterexamples distinguish algebraic tensors from actual metric curvature.
Inspected curvature-definition, coordinate-formula and contracted-Bianchi citations preserve signs and contractions. Matter conservation is conditional on the separately adopted field equation.
The scope remark uses divergence-free Einstein geometry with constant Λ and distinguishes it from a construction of gravitational energy or a no-go theorem.

Flat and linearized curvature use the same coordinate formula. Local-flatness L2 retains d(exp_p)_{tv}(tX)=J_X(t) on a star-shaped normal domain; the flat physical comparison retains the test-body qualifications.
First-order scalar and Einstein cross-checks correctly use vanishing background curvature. The flat quotient distinguishes invariant zero curvature from global Minkowski geometry.

Signs, contractions and frame-transformation formulas agree, but lem-gr-schwarzschild-ricci-and-einstein-tensors L3 overstates tensoriality as invariance of arbitrary component identities; routed in alerts.
FLRW curvature citations preserve the operator sign and Ricci contraction. Time-coordinate component conventions are stated, rather than inheriting length-coordinate units.

First-order contractions use the flat background correctly. Detector response identifies differential geodesic deviation rather than finite-pair acceleration, and distinguishes full mathematical geodesics from actual physical-history restrictions.

Constraint projections use the defined Einstein tensor. The contracted commutator and Raychaudhuri consumers retain the curvature sign and Ricci contraction; constant-component flatness is a zero-tensor conclusion.

Constraint and subsidiary-Bianchi citations are faithful, and the constant signature flip is explicitly derived. However, def-gr-dust-electric-magnetic-weyl-variables-and-schouten attributes Weyl terminology/decomposition to a supplier that supplies neither; routed in alerts.
